mathematics.scope: Fresh internal mathematical/editorial review of all four recursive Chapter 29 inputs, with the original read and two complete unchanged follow-up reads; cited external inputs retain their established scopes.

fresh_checks.check: Finite singularity volumes use the dominant Hermitian background and truncation; closed-background type invariance remains an explicitly cited input.
Lower monotonicity preserves the rooftop type by a low translate; upper monotonicity preserves the maximum type and exhausts off polar sets.
Volume addition gives a big sum background; subtraction inside the contact envelope recovers a competitor of the original type.
The deficit stretch requires b^n D < lower(v); its collapse contradiction uses near-maximal mass, a fixed truncation level and finite non-pluripolar tails.
The Lelong deficit bound uses one fixed modification and a common curvature bound; zero deficit allows arbitrarily large b.
Relative-envelope membership implies both volume equalities without positivity; the reverse uses positive lower reference volume.
Strict domination preserves the relative class after maximum replacement; contact coefficients force support on equality, and the fixed finite tail excludes collapse.
Exponential domination uses a strict gap before taking its limit; a global coefficient below one contradicts comparison with all translates.
Relative obstacle limits converge in capacity; ties are assigned to the fixed obstacle and the weighted lower-semicontinuity argument retains contact support.
Ordinary lower-volume equality includes zero volume; upper equality, relative membership and idempotence are asserted only under positive lower volume.
The small-stretch scale bounds all mixed masses in a dominant Hermitian background and makes the collapse error at most half the positive lower mass.
The strict barrier is below the potential; the smaller-background converse explicitly requires v-minus(theta)>0 for a uniform type-volume bound.
Lower background error comes from a mixed expansion and admissible competitors; the multiplicative comparison uses a strict lower potential and current addition.
Increasing envelope limits are identified by contact support before their volume is computed; the deficit then gives lower-volume and fixed-model Lelong continuity.
For decreasing models, a uniform small stretch retains a positive lower volume when the limiting lower bound is positive, using v-minus(Omega)>=ell.
Fixed-background decreasing volume continuity normalizes auxiliary ordinary envelopes before compactness and passes their convex inequalities to the limit.
Varying-background decrease uses corrected tail envelopes between q and q_j; uniform pullback curvature bounds justify fixed-model Lelong convergence.
The decreasing arbitrary-envelope criterion is precisely upper-volume continuity at positive lower volume; the constant-potential lower-volume limit needs no positivity.
Exact trace recovery explicitly assumes bounded mass on Y; the smaller-background majorant gives the uniform type-volume lower bound required on Y.
System recovery first proves the initial lower-volume identity, including zero; concavity propagates positive mass at each finite parameter without a uniform cutoff bound.
Local divisor errors in system recovery are controlled by uniform exponential integrability; compatibility and the all-local-model ideal criterion recover the system.
The maximum-volume comparison is finite, symmetric and type invariant; the basic upper-volume difference bound and ordered identity follow directly.
The zero-volume collapse example retains dimensions n>=2 for a closed background and n>=3 for a nonclosed bounded-mass background.
Positive-volume projection invariance uses the common maximum envelope; the normalized L1 estimate uses a fixed lower bound and normalized auxiliary models.
The three-point modulus handles the large-deficit branch by 2M and the small branch by the maximum convex inequality and 1-(1-t)^n<=nt.
Closed lower-volume sectors are Cauchy complete via successive tail maxima and decreasing normalized models; the modulus recovers the full original sequence.
The strict-cutoff curve example has mass 1-a and comparison |a-b|, so its only possible boundary mass is exactly delta.
Finite rooftops use a sum of upper-volume deficits below one positive lower bound; locality at a fixed truncation level produces the collapse contradiction.
Rooftop volume continuity first softens two genuine stretches, applies the finite-roof criterion, then squeezes both singularity volumes.
Capacity convergence uses ordinary finite rooftops, normalized decreasing limits and increasing lower bounds with retained positive lower volume; every subsequence is covered.
Dyadic ideal-volume limits compare equivalent analytic ordinary types term by term; upper-volume continuity retains its positive lower ideal-volume hypothesis.
The conditional ideal characterization separates zero-obstacle equality, upper-volume equality, relative membership and all-obstacle equality under positive lower ideal volume.
Fixed-big analytic correction uses rational convex coefficients and a strict analytic potential; the larger-background squeeze proves both volume and comparison limits.
The analytic closure criterion obtains a common lower-volume bound and L1 convergence before passing the normalized ideal-envelope convex bound to its limit.
Problem 29.8.1 remains unchanged; the adjacent nonclosed zero-volume example refutes upper-volume equality implying envelope equality but does not settle the other questions.
Smooth-gauge model comparison preserves currents and ordinary type after reprojection, with inverse gauge and preservation of analytic and ideal models.
Uniform one-sided background bounds share a fixed strict potential and mass bound; the three nonnegative errors give a factor 2, rather than a factor 4.
Analytic approximation with curvature error uses corrected rational analytic models and larger-background mass squeezes; convergence applies to canonical models.
The nearby-background lemma makes the strict reference theta-kappa*h/2 and comparison form common to both varying backgrounds.
Two-sided transport restores positivity and has c>=1/2; its larger background dominates theta+epsilon*h after scaling, giving the volume and comparison bounds.
Transport choice independence uses the minimum coefficient and maximum enlarged error; the minimum-attaining index supplies the necessary form domination.
The two-sided analytic criterion retains rational errors, produces a common positive lower-volume bound, and uses the uniform three-point modulus in a larger background.
The projective-plane triangle counterexample has masses (1-a)^2, (1-2a)^2 and 1-a^2; the two sides differ by 2a^2>0 after ordinary projection.
The lower-volume modulus uses positive reference mass and the deficit stretch; comparison convergence gives an eventual common positive lower-volume bound.
The complete metric entourages use reciprocal lower volumes and exponents a_(k+1)=n*a_k+1; the triple-composition estimate has the required power.
The chain bound splits at the first half-cost crossing and applies induction simultaneously at every dyadic scale; diagonal intersection gives separation.
Metric Cauchy sequences have bounded reciprocal lower volumes and therefore lie eventually in a closed positive sector; ideal models are closed and analytic models dense there.
Curve ordinary models are classified by positive polar curvature measures of mass at most the background area; bounded Green residue retains exactly that polar part.
The curve comparison equals total variation by the polar maximum formula, including zero mass; positive polar and atomic measure sets are closed under total-variation limits.
Curve metric convergence controls L1 and capacity at positive mass and, at zero mass, controls the full current by twice polar variation and harmonic uniqueness.
The moving-pole example converges away from capacity-small discs while its polar total-variation distance remains 2; weak currents alone need not give capacity convergence.
The nearest ideal model is the atomic part: diffuse polar mass is mutually singular to every signed atomic error, giving the exact defect and unique minimizer.
The diffuse Cantor construction has lengths exp(-4^(k+1)) and masses 2^(-k), forcing the Green potential to minus infinity on its polar support while all atoms vanish.
The ordinary curve topology includes atomic total variation and ordinary-envelope L1; finite large-atom sets and the floor formula establish all controlled ideal relations.
Canonical atomic loci are complete, not totally bounded for positive allowed mass; actual ordinary classes retain pseudometric nonuniqueness and strict positive-mass incompleteness.
Diffuse polar concentration is Cauchy in the ordinary-type topology at fixed positive mass but has no compatible limit; rotated disjoint supports distinguish polar variation.
The all-obstacle curve pseudometric uses a summable coordinate family and uniform ideal controls; equal polar curvature is exactly zero distance and atomic data give analytic closure.
The relative-envelope curve criterion includes full atomic mass by harmonic uniqueness; all-obstacle incompleteness uses averages under each fixed smooth obstacle.
Arbitrary positive-area curve backgrounds reduce by a smooth gauge; zero area leaves one smooth normalized potential and all envelope conditions hold.
Area homothety scales volume and total variation and commutes with atomic projection; analytic models are preserved only for rational area ratios under the stated convention.
Varying-background curve continuity uses a uniformly bounded Green inverse and the gauge oscillation estimate; zero-area collapse concerns the unscaled metric, while area-normalized data persist.
